samenvatting: Vandaag start het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat (EZK) de vernieuwde publiekscampagne Nieuwe Energie. De campagne laat zien hoe Nederlanders met eenvoudige keuzes energie kunnen besparen en slimmer gebruik kunnen maken van energie. Zo...
text:
Vandaag start het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat (EZK) de vernieuwde publiekscampagne Nieuwe Energie. De campagne laat zien hoe Nederlanders met eenvoudige keuzes energie kunnen besparen en slimmer gebruik kunnen maken van energie. Zo dragen we samen bij aan een betaalbaar, duurzaam en weerbaar energiesysteem.
Nederland werkt aan een nieuw energiesysteem waarin fossiele brandstoffen stap voor stap worden vervangen door duurzame energie uit wind en zon, kernenergie en waterstof. Daarmee maken we Nederland minder afhankelijk van fossiele energie uit het buitenland en bouwen we aan een energiesysteem dat klaar is voor de toekomst.
Die transitie kost tijd. Ook de komende jaren blijft Nederland deels afhankelijk van de import van olie en vloeibaar aardgas (LNG). Internationale ontwikkelingen kunnen daardoor invloed hebben op de beschikbaarheid en prijs van energie. De recente spanningen in het Midden-Oosten laten opnieuw zien hoe gebeurtenissen ver van huis ook in Nederland merkbaar kunnen zijn. Dat onderstreept het belang van een energiesysteem dat minder kwetsbaar is voor geopolitieke ontwikkelingen en beter bestand is tegen schommelingen op de internationale energiemarkt.
De campagne sluit aan bij het [Maatregelenpakket Acties Weerbaarheid Energieschok](https://www.rijksoverheid.nl/documenten/2026/04/20/actiesweerbaarheidenergieschok), dat het kabinet op 17 april presenteerde. Minder energie gebruiken helpt huishoudens en bedrijven hun energiekosten te verlagen, vermindert de druk op het elektriciteitsnet en maakt Nederland minder afhankelijk van energie uit het buitenland.
Minister Van Veldhoven, minister Klimaat en Groene Groei: "Voldoende en betaalbare energie is niet langer vanzelfsprekend. Dat hebben we de afgelopen periode gemerkt. Wat er in de wereld gebeurt, heeft gevolgen voor energieprijzen in Nederland. Het is daarom belangrijkom ons energiesysteem onafhankelijk te maken. Dat doen we onder andere door een systeem met zon- en windenergie te bouwen. Energie besparen is daarom altijd verstandig. Uiteindelijk is de goedkoopste energie, energie die je niet hoeft te gebruiken."
De campagne Nieuwe Energie laat zien dat we door te investeren in duurzame energie én zelf minder energie te gebruiken, we werken aan een sterker energiesysteem en Nederland minder afhankelijk maken van andere landen. Met eenvoudige handelingsperspectieven (zoals maximaal 5 minuten douchen en beter isoleren) helpen we mensen om energie besparen onderdeel te maken van het dagelijks leven. Juist kleine veranderingen kunnen al een verschil maken – voor de energierekening én voor een toekomstbestendige energievoorziening.
Ook de Rijksoverheid bespaart energie
De Rijksoverheid geeft zelf het goede voorbeeld en werkt aan een klimaatneutrale bedrijfsvoering. Dat gebeurt onder meer door rijksgebouwen te verduurzamen, energiezuiniger te maken en het gebruik van fossiele energie terug te dringen.
- Sinds 2019 is het aardgasverbruik van rijksgebouwen met ruim 30% afgenomen, onder meer door energiebesparende maatregelen en de verduurzaming van gebouwen.
- Inmiddels bestaat 35,5% van het civiele rijkswagenpark uit zero-emissievoertuigen. Doel is een volledig uitstootvrij wagenpark in 2028.
- De CO₂-uitstoot van dienstreizen per vliegtuig daalde afgelopen jaar met 14,6% ten opzichte van 2024.
- De Rijksoverheid investeert daarnaast in duurzame warmte, zoals de Warmte-Koude-Opslag voor het Binnenhof, en stimuleert de verduurzaming van productie- en energieketens.
De campagne loopt van 17 juli t/m 9 augustus via tv, radio, online (video en audio) social media en buitenreclame, en zal daarna online doorlopen tot 26 oktober 2026.

bron_titel: ‘A place of hope and solutions’: the building promising a better future
samenvatting: A bold new building in the Netherlands promises to showcase solutions to global problems – and encourage positive action The post ‘A place of hope and solutions’: the building promising a better future appeared first on Positive News .
text:
A bold new building in the Netherlands promises to showcase solutions to global problems – and encourage positive action
As briefs go, it’s an ambitious one: design a building that will accelerate the societal changes required to create a more sustainable future.
It’s a bold mission that appears to be one step closer after plans were unveiled for such a building on the banks of the river Maas in Rotterdam.
Billed as a place to help people “shift from complacency and powerlessness to hope, imagination and collective action for our shared future,” Shift Embassy promises to use the power of art, architecture and storytelling to showcase successful solutions to critical global challenges.
The refined design was unveiled on Tuesday after MVRDV won the international architecture competition for Shift Embassy.
The planned landmark will form part of Rotterdam’s new “nature-positive” Waterkant neighbourhood, which is expected to include 3,750 homes, schools and maker spaces built around a new tidal park.
The embassy was the brainchild of Shift, a social enterprise working to scale-up solutions to pressing global challenges. In an interview with Positive News, its founder Don Ritzen said that the idea behind the building is to create a hopeful vision of the future – and hasten the change needed to reach it.
“Most people, when they think about the future, they think that it’s all going to shit,” he said. “In order to bring more systemic change, we need to create places where people get inspired and get hope again, where they feel empowered to take action, and where they can meet like-minded people.”
Shift Embassy, he says, will be one such place. Inviting visitors to experience a sustainable future that has already arrived (albeit only in some parts of the world), it will use immersive art, inspiring stories and exhibitions to showcase alternative pathways to the ones humanity is on.
“We don’t believe in telling people what to do,” said Ritzen. “We believe in showing them what is possible, and that it’s something that they can participate in. It’s going to be fun.”
We need to create places where people get inspired and get hope again
MVRDV was chosen to design Shift Embassy after its proposal, dubbed Rotterdam Rocks, was taken forward by a judging panel. The plans will now be put out to a public consultation, before the necessary construction permits are sought.
MVRDV’s renders depict a rocky, vegetation-strewn landmark on the banks of the Maas. Featuring a giant exhibition space showcasing “global success stories in nature, energy, travel, and circularity”, the building will also contain educational spaces, places for community events and a hotel.
“Rotterdam Rocks departs from how sustainability is traditionally communicated, bringing together joy, discovery, and surprise into a new architectural language,” said the judges. “We anticipate this building and its programme will invite people to rethink their everyday behaviour and encourage new ways of living sustainably together.”
Winy Maas, a founding partner of MVRDV, said that the project will also serve as a “scale-up lab” to showcase the latest innovations in low-carbon construction.
“We need to reduce carbon dioxide emissions and to create inclusive spaces for people, trees, plants, for water, air, and for animal habitats, balancing the need for new built space with new landscapes to compensate our ecological impact,” he said. “Our design integrates these human and natural spaces.”

bron_titel: ‘It’s brought a sense of community back to the town’
samenvatting: A growing backlash against the Premier League has sparked huge interest in community clubs, which make football affordable for everyone The post ‘It’s brought a sense of community back to the town’ appeared first on Positive News .
text:
As Premier League prices rise, growing numbers of supporters are seeking out something closer, cheaper and more human in non-league football
It is just after three o’clock on a hot bank holiday Monday in Spalding, Lincolnshire, and the Sir Halley Stewart Playing Field is rammed with more than 2,700 supporters squeezing into the ground. Nearly 500 of them have travelled from Bedford to watch Real Bedford, a club that did not exist in its current form until a few years ago, try to take one more unlikely step up the football pyramid.
In 2021, local entrepreneur and podcaster Peter McCormack bought Bedford FC, then playing in the 10th tier, renamed it Real Bedford and began talking about taking his hometown club all the way. Since then, Real Bedford have won three successive promotions, attracted significant investment, and made Bedford, one of England’s largest towns without a professional football club, feel as if it might finally have a team with proper momentum behind it.
“Bedford has always had the people, the pride and the appetite for football, but it never had a club that matched the size of the town,” says McCormack. “The ambition is huge, but it has to feel local first. If people in Bedford don’t feel this belongs to them, then it doesn’t work.”
For supporters such as Andy Chinneck, who also follows Manchester United, the appeal is not only the football but the feeling around it. “At United, unless you’re lucky, wealthy or very organised, you can feel like a customer at a global entertainment business,” he says. “At Real Bedford, I can turn up with mates, have a pint, stand near the pitch and feel like I’m actually part of the club. Having lived in Bedford most of my life it feels like it’s brought a much needed sense of local community back to the town.”
The frustration with Premier League football has been building for years. The Football Supporters’ Association says the cost of attending top-flight football rose well above inflation in the late-1990s and early-2000s, and its recent work on ticket prices found that 19 of 20 Premier League clubs increased prices in 2024/25, with 13 doing so again in 2025/26. Its research also found that Premier League ticket prices have risen 20% since Covid, according to the league’s own data, and that 71% of fans believe traditional supporters are being priced out.
Ownership has sharpened that feeling with American billionaires, Middle East investment funds and international consortiums owning most of the Premier League teams. The clubs themselves are now enormous assets, with recent estimates putting Manchester United worth more than £4bn, Manchester City and Liverpool close behind, and Arsenal above £3bn.
The backlash to this model led to the creation of FC United of Manchester in 2005. Founded by Manchester United supporters who believed that “football had lost its way”, and were angry at American billionaire businessman Malcolm Glazer taking over their club, they decided to set up their own.
FC United is member-owned, built around a one-member, one-vote model. It has 2,475 co-owners, including 2,137 adult members and 338 junior members.
“We are making football affordable for ordinary football supporters,” says FC United spokesman Jules Spencer. “Many of us can no longer afford to go to Premier League games with our families, but we can afford to go and watch FC United where the quality of entertainment on offer in non-league football is real value for money.”
It feels like it’s brought a much needed sense of local community back to the town
The club has since risen to the seventh tier of the football pyramid, and regularly sees gates of well over 3,000 – making it one of the highest-attended teams in non-league.
Across the country, the same pull is showing up in the numbers. Attendances in National League South hit a 10-year high in 2024/25, with an average crowd of 1,221, up 134% on 2014/15, while the Isthmian Premier Division averaged 764, a 94% rise over the same period.
“People want to watch non-league football because they are discovering that it’s a lot better than they think,” says James Doe, founder of Non-League Day, a day set aside in English football where supporters of clubs playing at the highest levels of the game are encouraged to experience football at non-league level. “It’s very accessible – clubs are nearby, admission, food and drink are affordable, it’s far more child friendly and you can get really close to the action. You can even change ends at half time,” he says.
“For many people, football has been something they’ve only ever enjoyed on television and it’s often been marketed in a way that teaches them there is nothing else. When you go to a local club you realise that’s not the case and can quickly get hooked. Why stay at home when you can be out with your friends being part of something?” says Doe.
Back in Spalding, Real Bedford look as if they are about to add another chapter to that argument. They are 2-1 up with minutes to go, close enough to see the sixth tier opening in front of them, before a controversial late penalty drags Spalding level and extra time does the rest. Real lose 4-2, their fourth straight promotion postponed for at least another year, but the noise from the away end suggests something important has already happened.
Photography by Curt Taylor

bron_titel: Leopards recover in Zambia as communities swap skins for synthetics
samenvatting: Replacing real leopard skins with synthetic furs has helped leopards recover in western Zambia, researchers say The post Leopards recover in Zambia as communities swap skins for synthetics appeared first on Positive News .
text:
Conservationists say a switch from real leopard skins to synthetic furs in traditional ceremonies has helped reduce poaching and boost leopard numbers in western Zambia
Big cat conservationists in Zambia say leopard numbers are rebounding thanks in part to local communities swapping real furs for synthetic in traditional ceremonies.
Leopards are revered by cultural and religious groups which use their prized pelts as ceremonial regalia.
In western Zambia, during an annual event marking the onset of the flood season, 200 paddlers ferry the king of the Lozi people, the Litunga, on a barge. They wear skirts fashioned largely from leopard skins, and demand for the striking outfits is believed to have been one of the drivers of leopard poaching.
Now the tide appears to be turning following a programme led by the global wild cat conservation organisation, [Panthera](https://panthera.org/).
Consulting with communities, the organisation sourced quality synthetic furs, coined Heritage Furs, and secured a royal stamp of approval, with the Litunga decreeing that only Heritage Furs should be worn in official ceremonies.
The shift to Heritage Furs could save between 204 and 1,310 leopards in the region over a decade
Across southern Africa, Panthera has supplied more than 22,000 Heritage Furs, but in-depth evaluation of the initiative’s impact has been limited until now. Fresh research published in the journal Conservation Biology shows that leopard numbers in western Zambia are recovering, poaching incidents are down, and just 10% of the Litunga’s paddlers favour real furs over the alternative.
The collaborative study involving numerous organisations suggests that a shift to Heritage Furs could save between 204 and 1,310 leopards in the region over a decade, while also acknowledging the role of counter-trafficking measures and enforcement in the conservation success.
Lead author and Panthera scientist Aditya Shekhar Malgaonkar wrote: “Our results provide the first empirical link between a demand-reduction initiative based on synthetic substitutes and measurable population recovery of species.”

text:
Cheetahs are back in Zambia’s Greater Luangwa Ecosystem, nearly 30 years after the big cats’ last recorded presence in the massive landscape.
Six cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus), three males and three females, were earlier in July moved by Zambia’s Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW) and several conservation groups, including the South Africa-based Endangered Wildlife Trust (EWT), to a remote part of North Luangwa National Park.
The cheetahs were translocated from private reserves in South Africa. Another six will be moved in August, while a third batch of six will follow in August 2027, according to a statement by EWT.
There haven’t been confirmed sightings of cheetahs in the Greater Luangwa Ecosystem since 1998, according to EWT’s fact sheet, which attributes the cat’s disappearance to successive outbreaks of anthrax disease and habitat disturbance.
“Many of the threats that likely contributed to the disappearance of cheetahs from Luangwa in the 1990s have been significantly reduced,” Olivia Sievert, manager for EWT’s Cheetah Metapopulation Project, told Mongabay by email.
Sievert said conservation efforts in North Luangwa and South Luangwa national parks, the two major protected areas in the ecosystem, have resulted in healthy prey populations, allowing large carnivores such as lions (Panthera leo) and African wild dogs (Lycaon pictus) to flourish across the ecosystem.
“However, cheetahs are unable to naturally recolonise the Luangwa valley because the nearest viable populations are too distant and disconnected for natural dispersal to occur,” Sievert said. “As a result, active reintroduction is the only realistic way to restore the species to this part of its historic range.”
Southern Africa is an important stronghold for cheetahs, listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. However, their populations here continue to decline because of habitat fragmentation and expanding farmland.
“By establishing another viable population in southern Africa, the project strengthens the overall resilience, genetic security and long-term conservation prospects of cheetahs worldwide,” Sievert said.
Nakedi Maputla, director for species, conservation and planning at the nonprofit African Wildlife Foundation, who isn’t involved in the initiative, told Mongabay there’s a mixed record of cheetah translocations in Africa: some have successfully established breeding populations, as in [Malawi](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/oryx/article/assessing-the-success-of-the-first-cheetah-reintroduction-in-malawi/18DCB2DD6FA1C7DE2B61DF60DC449837); others, such as in Zimbabwe’s [Matusadona](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/oryx/article/reassessment-of-an-introduced-cheetah-acinonyx-jubatus-population-in-matusadona-national-park-zimbabwe/163848EED4B2F49F81C65E306E6735B0), have failed due to poor planning and lack of long-term monitoring.
Maputla said successfully reestablishing a cheetah population in North Luangwa will depend on “habitat upkeep, tracking movements, conflict mitigation, and enhanced engagement with local communities, as cheetah recovery is both social and ecological.”
Sievert said there’s low risk of conflict in Luangwa between cheetahs and people living around the ecosystem, given that livelihoods there center mainly on crops and poultry rather than livestock, which are often targeted by the cats.
“Extensive community consultations have already been undertaken to build local understanding and support,” she said.

references.text: Introduction Global expansion of the human population has resulted in rapid declines of biodiversity (Ceballos et al., [Reference Ceballos, Ehrlich and Raven2020](https://www.cambridge.org#ref14)). To offset biodiversity losses, reintroductions and translocations are increasingly used to re-establish wildlife populations in areas where they were previously extirpated (Bubac et al., [Reference Bubac, Johnson, Fox and Cullingham2019](https://www.cambridge.org#ref11)). Large carnivores have experienced dramatic contractions of their geographical range and subsequent population declines in the past 2 centuries (Ripple et al., [Reference Ripple, Estes, Beschta, Wilmers, Ritchie and Hebblewhite2014](https://www.cambridge.org#ref41)). They are now amongst the most commonly reintroduced taxa (Seddon et al., [Reference Seddon, Soorae and Launay2005](https://www.cambridge.org#ref44)), with reintroductions aiming to recover parts of their historical ranges and restore ecosystem functions (Ripple et al., [Reference Ripple, Estes, Beschta, Wilmers, Ritchie and Hebblewhite2014](https://www.cambridge.org#ref41); Atkins et al., [Reference Atkins, Long, Pansu, Daskin, Potter and Stalmans2019](https://www.cambridge.org#ref2)). In South Africa, the historical loss of wildlife, and the potential financial value of large carnivores through ecotourism (Di Minin et al., [Reference Di Minin, Fraser, Slotow and MacMillan2013](https://www.cambridge.org#ref17)), have led to an increase in reintroductions into fenced protected areas (Hayward et al., [Reference Hayward, Adendorff, O'Brien, Sholto-Douglas, Bissett and Moolman2007a](https://www.cambridge.org#ref27)). A managed metapopulation approach has resulted in population increases in lions Panthera leo (Ferreira & Hofmeyer, [Reference Ferreira and Hofmeyr2014](https://www.cambridge.org#ref20)), cheetahs Acinonyx jubatus (Buk et al., [Reference Buk, van der Merwe, Marnewick and Funston2018](https://www.cambridge.org#ref12)) and African wild dogs Lycaon pictus (Davies-Mostert et al., [Reference Davies-Mostert, Mills and Macdonald2015](https://www.cambridge.org#ref16)), and has provided opportunities to expand the ranges of large carnivores in various countries. Although pre-release procedures for carnivores have been refined over time to maximize success (e.g. so-called soft releases; Hayward et al., [Reference Hayward, Adendorff, O'Brien, Sholto-Douglas, Bissett and Moolman2007a](https://www.cambridge.org#ref27)), few studies have evaluated post-reintroduction movements, settlement and their effects on the early establishment of founder populations (Hunter, [Reference Hunter1998](https://www.cambridge.org#ref30); Yiu et al., [Reference Yiu, Keith, Karczmarski and Parrini2015](https://www.cambridge.org#ref48); Briers-Louw et al., [Reference Briers-Louw, Verschueren and Leslie2019](https://www.cambridge.org#ref10)). Successful population establishment requires the settlement of a sufficient number of dispersing individuals that go on to develop a viable population based on the species’ life histories (Hovestadt & Poethke, [Reference Hovestadt and Poethke2005](https://www.cambridge.org#ref29)). Reintroductions are essentially forced dispersals; translocated animals have to adjust to novel resources and environmental conditions (Berger-Tal & Saltz, [Reference Berger-Tal and Saltz2014](https://www.cambridge.org#ref4)), and balance a trade-off between exploration and exploitation of their new habitat (Stamps & Swaisgood, [Reference Stamps and Swaisgood2007](https://www.cambridge.org#ref45)). Translocations may fail if released individuals range over large areas, do not establish individual home ranges or have low survival and reproductive rates (Armstrong & Seddon, [Reference Armstrong and Seddon2007](https://www.cambridge.org#ref1); Stamps & Swaisgood, [Reference Stamps and Swaisgood2007](https://www.cambridge.org#ref45)). Therefore, careful monitoring of early post-release movements and population establishment is crucial to assess reintroduction success (Armstrong & Seddon, [Reference Armstrong and Seddon2007](https://www.cambridge.org#ref1)). Cheetahs were extirpated in Malawi by the early 1990s (Purchase & Purchase, [Reference Purchase and Purchase2007](https://www.cambridge.org#ref38)). In 2015 a public–private partnership between African Parks and the Malawi Department of National Parks and Wildlife to manage Liwonde National Park (hereafter Liwonde) made reintroductions of large carnivores possible. Liwonde was selected to be the first protected area to reintroduce cheetahs in Malawi as it was well protected and harboured an abundant prey base (7,296 small to medium-sized antelopes counted in a 2016 aerial survey; C. Reid, pers. comm., 2019) and depleted competitor populations (an estimated 25 spotted hyenas Crocuta crocuta, and initially no lions or leopards Panthera pardus; C. Reid, pers. comm., 2019). Here, we investigated the early post-release movements, settlement, survival and reproduction of seven cheetahs reintroduced to Liwonde. We expected distances of daily movements to be highest immediately after release, with a decrease over time and subsequent stability. Stabilization of daily movement distances, and movements within a gradually more confined area are indicative of home range development (Börger & Fryxell, [Reference Börger, Fryxell, Clobert, Baguette, Benton and Bullock2012](https://www.cambridge.org#ref8)) and thus indicate settlement. We also compared survival and reproduction parameters to those of source populations to examine population establishment and early-stage reintroduction success. Study area We monitored post-release movements of reintroduced cheetahs in Liwonde National Park in southern Malawi ([Fig. 1](https://www.cambridge.org#fig01)). The Park covers 548 km2 and its boundary is fenced with a 2.4-m high fence (Bonnox, Johannesburg, South Africa) consisting of eight electric wires. Maximum temperature ranges from 28 °C in July to 40 °C in November, and mean annual rainfall is 944 mm, primarily occurring during December–March (Bhima & Dudley, [Reference Bhima and Dudley1996](https://www.cambridge.org#ref5)). In the wet season, the perennial Shire River, which runs through the Park, creates extensive lagoons and marshlands on its floodplains. Only a few pools of water remain scattered throughout the Park by September, the peak of the dry season. Dry deciduous woodland with Colophospermum mopane occupies the majority of the Park. Methods Pre-release management A total of seven cheetahs (four males and three females; [Table 1](https://www.cambridge.org#tab01)) were released in Liwonde in various combinations on four occasions during June 2017–February 2018. To ensure genetic diversity of the founder population, cheetahs were sourced from five protected areas in South Africa through the Endangered Wildlife Trust's Cheetah Metapopulation Project. Prior to release, three females and two males were fitted with Pinnacle LITE GPS satellite collars (465 g; Sirtrack, Hawkes Bay, New Zealand), and one male within a coalition of two related males was fitted with a VHF tracking collar (253 g; African Wildlife Tracking, Pretoria, South Africa). Collars weighed 0.4–1.3% of the animals’ body weight. All individuals were kept in temporary holding enclosures (bomas; 50 × 50 m) for 23–58 days before being released into the reserve. A group of three siblings was held together in a boma, as were two non-sibling individuals, CF1 and CM1. CF1 had been orphaned and subsequently captured for relocation at a young age, and it was hoped the bonding afforded by co-housing with CM1 would facilitate reintroduction success for CF1. Once individuals no longer demonstrated stress behaviours such as pacing, they were released from the boma through coaxing with a final feed, and the gate was closed to ensure they did not return to the boma. All origin locations are in South Africa. 5 Damage to collar prevented the download of data. Post-release monitoring We tracked the cheetahs’ post-release movements during June 2017–July 2019. GPS collars collected a minimum of three GPS fixes per day (at 05.00, 06.00, 12.00). Frequency of GPS fixes was increased when animals had cubs or were injured, to monitor them more closely during these periods. To assess survival, we checked physical condition at least twice per week, locating cheetahs through VHF tracking (receiver: Communication Specialists, Orange, USA; H-Type antenna: Telonics, Mesa, USA). We supplemented these observations with opportunistic sightings. We also inspected dens within the first 2 weeks of denning to record location, litter size and cub survival. To minimize disturbance, dens were checked by a single person while the female was hunting, and we did not handle the cubs (Laurenson & Caro, [Reference Laurenson and Caro1994](https://www.cambridge.org#ref32)). Introduction As a consequence of increasing human populations and the resulting demand for agricultural land and pressure on natural resources, the ranges of most large carnivores have contracted substantially (Di Minin et al., [Reference Di Minin, Slotow, Hunter, Montesino Pouzols, Toivonen and Verburg2016](https://www.cambridge.org#ref7)). Maintaining viable populations of large carnivores requires large connected habitat networks (Di Minin et al., [Reference Di Minin, Slotow, Hunter, Montesino Pouzols, Toivonen and Verburg2016](https://www.cambridge.org#ref7)). However, such networks are often inhabited by people, who degrade carnivore habitat and persecute large carnivores because of actual or perceived livestock losses, confining them to isolated patches of land (Di Minin et al., [Reference Di Minin, Slotow, Hunter, Montesino Pouzols, Toivonen and Verburg2016](https://www.cambridge.org#ref7)). Translocation is regularly used to mitigate conflict, secure viability of isolated populations and reintroduce populations in former or new range (Linnell et al., [Reference Linnell, Aanes and Swenson1997](https://www.cambridge.org#ref17); Fischer & Lindenmayer, [Reference Fischer and Lindenmayer2000](https://www.cambridge.org#ref10)). Success depends on the aim of the translocation, the source of the translocated individuals, the number of individuals released and the cause of the original decline (Fischer & Lindenmayer, [Reference Fischer and Lindenmayer2000](https://www.cambridge.org#ref10)). Translocations generally fail to reduce human–carnivore conflict and it is now widely accepted that such negative interactions are best mitigated by promoting coexistence (Linnell et al., [Reference Linnell, Aanes and Swenson1997](https://www.cambridge.org#ref17); Fischer & Lindenmayer, [Reference Fischer and Lindenmayer2000](https://www.cambridge.org#ref10); Boast et al., [Reference Boast, Chelysheva, van der Merwe, Schmidt- Küntzel, Walker, Cilliers, Boast and Schmidt-Küntzel2018a](https://www.cambridge.org#ref1)). However, translocations to establish or re-establish and augment populations of native, non-vulnerable, wildlife species seem more successful (Griffith et al., [Reference Griffith, Scott, Carpenter and Reed1989](https://www.cambridge.org#ref12)). Translocation success increases when the source population is wild, the founder population is large (Griffith et al., [Reference Griffith, Scott, Carpenter and Reed1989](https://www.cambridge.org#ref12); Fischer & Lindenmayer, [Reference Fischer and Lindenmayer2000](https://www.cambridge.org#ref10)) and the original cause of the population decline has been eliminated (Fischer & Lindenmayer, [Reference Fischer and Lindenmayer2000](https://www.cambridge.org#ref10)). Although it is recognized that monitoring is crucial to improve the success of translocations (IUCN/SSC, [2013](https://www.cambridge.org#ref15)), there has been little follow-up of translocated animals to determine success (Linnell et al., [Reference Linnell, Aanes and Swenson1997](https://www.cambridge.org#ref17)) and long-term evaluation of introduced or reintroduced populations is often lacking (Fischer & Lindenmayer, [Reference Fischer and Lindenmayer2000](https://www.cambridge.org#ref10)). The cheetah is a large carnivore species regularly translocated for conservation purposes (Boast et al., [Reference Boast, Chelysheva, van der Merwe, Schmidt- Küntzel, Walker, Cilliers, Boast and Schmidt-Küntzel2018a](https://www.cambridge.org#ref1)). A relatively well-documented translocation is the 1993–1994 translocation of alleged problem cheetahs from commercial farmland into Matusadona National Park, Zimbabwe, an unfenced protected area without resident cheetahs (Zank, [Reference Zank1995](https://www.cambridge.org#ref32); Pitman, [Reference Pitman2007](https://www.cambridge.org#ref21)). Although it was initially thought the introduced cheetah population would not be viable without intensive management (Zank, [Reference Zank1995](https://www.cambridge.org#ref32)), it persisted without intervention and, with the establishment of a breeding population, the introduction was cautiously deemed a success (Purchase & Vhurumuku, [Reference Purchase and Vhurumuku2005](https://www.cambridge.org#ref24)). Whether the translocation reduced human–cheetah conflict on commercial farmland is unknown (Purchase, [Reference Purchase1998](https://www.cambridge.org#ref22)). In this study, we used citizen science, questionnaire-based information, camera-trap and spoor surveys to reassess the status of Matusadona's cheetah population and model current cheetah occupancy in relation to densities of competing carnivores and terrain elevation. Our follow-up highlights the importance of thorough planning and standardized long-term monitoring of translocated populations to understand the factors affecting translocation success and to improve future translocation programmes. Study area and species The 1,370 km2 unfenced Matusadona National Park, utilized for photographic safaris, lies in northern Zimbabwe on the shore of Lake Kariba. Depending on the lake level, the Park comprises a valley of c. 400 km2 and an escarpment of c. 1,000 km2 ([Fig. 1](https://www.cambridge.org#fig01)). During 1993–1994, 21 alleged problem cheetahs were opportunistically removed from commercial farmland in southern Zimbabwe; six died shortly after capture, and 15 were kept in a captive enclosure (boma) for 6 weeks and then soft released into the Park, which held no resident cheetahs at the time (Zank, [Reference Zank1995](https://www.cambridge.org#ref32); Pitman, [Reference Pitman2007](https://www.cambridge.org#ref21)). Although it was assumed cheetahs were once resident in Matusadona, there are no records to support this (Zank, [Reference Zank1995](https://www.cambridge.org#ref32)) and it remains unknown whether cheetahs had become extinct or had never been present at all (Purchase, [Reference Purchase1998](https://www.cambridge.org#ref22)). The introduced cheetahs utilized only the valley floor (Purchase, [Reference Purchase1998](https://www.cambridge.org#ref22)), which has a grassland foreshore but largely consists of woodland with Colophospermum mopane, Combretum spp. and Terminalia spp. The escarpment is dominated by miombo woodland and is characterized by steep valleys with limited water availability in the dry season (Zank, [Reference Zank1995](https://www.cambridge.org#ref32); Purchase, [Reference Purchase1998](https://www.cambridge.org#ref22)). The cheetah's competitors, lion Panthera leo, leopard Panthera pardus and spotted hyaena Crocuta crocuta, occur in the Park. For Matusadona's large carnivores, buffalo Syncerus caffer and impala Aepyceros melampus have historically been the most abundant prey species (Zank, [Reference Zank1995](https://www.cambridge.org#ref32); Purchase, [Reference Purchase2004](https://www.cambridge.org#ref23)). The Park is bordered by the Sanyati and Ume rivers and surrounded by communal land used for subsistence farming and trophy hunting under the Communal Areas Management Programme for Indigenous Resources (CAMPFIRE; [Fig. 1](https://www.cambridge.org#fig01)). Methods Data collection As part of a nationwide survey (van der Meer, [Reference van der Meer2018](https://www.cambridge.org#ref28)), we launched a citizen science programme (2012–present) to collect cheetah sightings and photographs from tourists, safari operators and others. In addition, we interviewed 49 respondents (August–September 2013) about cheetah presence in Matusadona and surrounding areas: 23 Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority rangers, seven CAMPFIRE rangers, six safari guides, five hunters and eight hunting scouts (van der Meer, [Reference van der Meer2018](https://www.cambridge.org#ref28)). If respondents had seen cheetahs, we recorded sighting date and location, number of individuals, age, sex and size. We only included sightings from respondents who could identify the cheetah from carnivore pictures and clearly recalled sighting details. Some respondents provided photographs with their sightings. We also asked respondents about human–cheetah conflict and anthropogenic cheetah mortality, and checked reports at the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority and CAMPFIRE offices for records of conflict and mortality. During June–August 2016 we carried out a camera-trap survey using a pre-planned grid of 49 traps set up 4–5 km apart on the valley floor and part of the escarpment ([Fig. 1](https://www.cambridge.org#fig01)). Each trap station consisted of two Cuddeback (Cuddeback, Wisconsin, USA) or Panthera V2 (Panthera, New York, USA) cameras, c. 6 m apart, facing each other but slightly offset, to limit interference from the flash. The cameras were attached to trees or metal standards c. 60 cm above ground level. Following establishment, the survey was run for 40 days, after which traps were removed within the same time frame and order in which they were deployed. In June 2013 we drove three road transects on the valley floor (total length 59.8 km), and in July–August 2016 we drove four road transects on the valley floor (total length 68.2 km), all of which were driven three times in the early morning, on different days, and three of which repeated routes surveyed in 2013. Transects were driven at 10–20 km/h, with an experienced tracker on a seat mounted at the front of the vehicle. Hawaiian stilt population improves from 200 to in 40s to 1,500 today, recovery documented in UH study
The US Fish and Wildlife Service announced the reclassification of the Aeʻo, or Hawaiian stilt (Himantopus mexicanus knudseni), from endangered to threatened under the Endangered Species Act, a rare and hopeful milestone for a native Hawaiian species.
The change, published in the Federal Register alongside a species-specific 4(d) rule, reflects more than 50 years of conservation work that has brought the long-legged waterbird back from the brink.
The recovery is documented in a new study led by researchers from the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s [College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience](https://cms.ctahr.hawaii.edu/) (CTAHR) and their partners, published in [Ornithological Applications](https://doi.org/10.1093/ornithapp/duag037). 
Once abundant across the Hawaiian Islands, the Aeʻo dwindled to roughly 200 birds in the 1940s after decades of overhunting, the loss of wetlands to agriculture and development, and the spread of invasive predators. Following its listing as endangered in 1973 and sustained conservation efforts, the population has since climbed to more than 1,500 birds today.
Community partnering with conservation managers
The team analyzed more than five decades of data, representing more than 2,000 nests across nine wetlands on Oʻahu from 1963 to 2020. They found that nesting success and chick fledging success improved measurably over time, providing evidence that management actions such as predator control and habitat restoration are working.
“This is a bright spot story,” said Melissa Price, associate professor in CTAHR’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Management. “So many species across Hawaiʻi are in decline. The ae‘o demonstrates how community can work in partnership with conservation managers to achieve recovery and rebuild relationships with our native species.”
A promising path
Expanding managed wetland habitat is the key to increasing the Ae‘o population. Ae‘o readily colonize restored and managed wetlands, and recent work has documented the birds nesting in restored Indigenous wetland agro-ecosystems. As sea-level rise threatens existing coastal wetlands, these community- and culturally-grounded restoration efforts offer both new habitat and a model for stewardship.
The new rule accompanying the reclassification is designed to keep the momentum going. It allows certain activities that benefit the Aeʻo to continue, including habitat management and restoration work, even where such activities would otherwise be restricted under the Act. This flexibility is intended to sustain the partnerships and on-the-ground care that the species still depends on as it progresses toward full recovery.
The authors are careful to call the Ae‘o a “conservation success story in progress.” Like many native Hawaiian species, it remains conservation-reliant: dependent on ongoing predator control, water management and habitat protection.
“Downlisting doesn’t mean the work is done,” said lead author Jessica Idle, a manager with the UH Mānoa Pacific Cooperative Studies Unit. “It means the work is paying off. Continued monitoring and management, especially expanding protected wetland habitat, will be essential to keep the population growing.”
The research was a collaboration among UH Mānoa, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources, Tufts University and other partners, reflecting the coordinated, cross-agency effort behind the bird’s recovery.
